title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
Tenant Thread operates through a multi-agent environment in which employees, personal agents, office systems, and external platforms interact through a large number of automated events. These interactions include email access, file access, task delegation, calendar scheduling, advice generation, and public posting activities.
The key incident examined in this report is an anomalous post sent to SaidIT by John Windward on May 17, 2046, at approximately 4:21 AM. The incident raises an important operational question: was the post caused by a single isolated mistake, or was it the visible outcome of a broader failure pattern within the multi-agent system?
Rather than treating the anomalous post as an isolated text-quality issue, this report reconstructs the underlying event chain. The analysis examines how instructions, files, people, agents, and systems interacted before the post was released. It also compares the latest incident with earlier suspicious behaviours to identify whether similar warning signals appeared previously.



The purpose of this report is to use visual analytics to trace the origin and propagation of the anomalous SaidIT post. The analysis focuses on four objectives:

Reconstruct the exact sequence of events that led to the public post.
Identify the people, agents, files, and systems involved in the event chain.
Compare the latest incident with earlier suspicious behaviours.
Recommend one targeted intervention point that could reduce the likelihood of recurrence.




This report addresses the following questions:

How was the anomalous SaidIT post generated?
Which people, personal agents, and systems were involved?
What was the confirmed content source of the post?
Did similar suspicious behaviours occur before the latest incident?
Where should the system intervene to prevent similar public releases?

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
2.1 Analytical Approach
This investigation follows a staged visual analytics workflow.
The first stage prepares and audits the raw JSON data. The second stage extracts suspicious instruction-file handoffs. The third stage reconstructs the latest incident and compares it with earlier suspicious chains. The final stage evaluates one targeted intervention point.
This staged approach is important because the event log contains nested and heterogeneous records. Different event types contain different detail fields. Therefore, the analysis preserves the original JSON structure first and only extracts selected fields when they are needed for a specific analytical purpose.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
2.2 Analytical Tools
The analysis is conducted in R using Quarto for reproducible reporting.
The packages loaded at this stage support JSON import, data wrangling, timestamp conversion, visualisation, and interactive tables. Network-analysis packages will be added in a later section when the actor-level interaction tables are ready.


Show the code
if (!requireNamespace("pacman", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pacman")
}

pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  jsonlite,
  lubridate,
  janitor,
  scales,
  DT,
  DiagrammeR
)

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(
    base_size = 13
  )
)

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
2.3 Data Sources
The investigation uses two JSON files.

MC2 data.json contains the internal event timeline. Each record represents an action performed by a person, personal agent, office system, or external platform.
org_chart.json contains the Tenant Thread organization structure, including departments, teams, people, and reporting relationships.

The file paths are stored as reusable objects before data import. This avoids repeatedly hard-coding folder locations and improves reproducibility when the project is rendered or published.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
3.1 Importing the Raw JSON Files
The two JSON files are imported without simplifying nested structures.
This choice is deliberate. The event log contains a details object whose structure changes across event types. For example, a file-access event may store a file path, while a task-delegation event may store a target agent and a nested task argument.
To avoid losing information during import, the original nested structure is preserved. The raw objects are retained throughout the analysis so that later derived tables can always be traced back to the original records.


Show the code
mc2_raw <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  mc2_path,
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)

org_raw <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  org_path,
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
3.3 Creating the Raw Event Table
The event records are converted into a tibble with six core variables:

event_order: the original record order in the JSON timeline;
id: the unique event identifier;
short_name: the action performed;
when: the original Unix timestamp;
parties: the people, agents, or systems involved;
details: additional nested information associated with the event.

The event_order variable is important because multiple automated actions may occur within the same second. It preserves the original sequence of records even when timestamps are identical.
The parties and details variables are intentionally retained as list-columns. This preserves the original event structure and avoids prematurely flattening fields that may not exist for every event type.


Show the code
events_raw <- tibble(
  event_order = seq_along(
    mc2_raw$events
  ),
  id = map_int(
    mc2_raw$events,
    ~ .x$id
  ),
  short_name = map_chr(
    mc2_raw$events,
    ~ .x$short_name
  ),
  when = map_dbl(
    mc2_raw$events,
    ~ .x$when
  ),
  parties = map(
    mc2_raw$events,
    ~ .x$parties
  ),
  details = map(
    mc2_raw$events,
    ~ .x$details
  )
)

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
3.4 Standardising Timestamp Variables
The raw when variable is stored as a Unix timestamp.
To support reproducible sequence analysis, the timestamps are converted into both UTC time and local time. UTC time is retained as the standard reference. Local time is created using the America/Los_Angeles time zone because the incident description refers to an anomalous SaidIT post sent at approximately 4:21 AM local time.
The analysis also creates date-level and hour-level variables. These variables will later support timeline visualisations, historical comparisons, and incident-window filtering.


Show the code
events_clean <- events_raw %>%
  mutate(
    timestamp_utc = as_datetime(
      when,
      tz = "UTC"
    ),
    timestamp_local = with_tz(
      timestamp_utc,
      tzone = "America/Los_Angeles"
    ),
    event_date_local = as_date(
      timestamp_local
    ),
    event_hour_local = floor_date(
      timestamp_local,
      unit = "hour"
    ),
    party_count = map_int(
      parties,
      length
    )
  )

glimpse(
  events_clean
)

section: 3.10 Visualising the Most Frequent Event Types
text:
3.10 Visualising the Most Frequent Event Types
The most frequent event types are visualised to establish a high-level system baseline.
Incident-relevant actions are highlighted. These actions may not dominate the full dataset, but they require closer inspection because they may form part of the propagation chain that led to the public SaidIT post.


Show the code
event_type_summary %>%
  slice_head(
    n = 12
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    short_name = fct_reorder(
      short_name,
      n
    ),
    incident_relevant = short_name %in% c(
      "queue_subordinate_task",
      "delete_file",
      "saidit_post",
      "saidit_post_check"
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = n,
      y = short_name,
      fill = incident_relevant
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.72,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE" = "#E76F51",
      "FALSE" = "#5DADE2"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = comma
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Most Frequent Event Types in the Multi-Agent System",
    subtitle = "Incident-relevant actions are highlighted",
    x = "Number of Events",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(
    base_size = 13
  )









The event-type distribution establishes the system baseline. Routine automated actions dominate the event log. Incident-relevant actions are less frequent but require closer investigation because they may form part of the propagation chain that led to the public SaidIT post.

3.12 Inspecting the Immediate Incident Window

    event_order,
    id,
    timestamp_local,
    short_name,

The first two phases establish a reproducible analytical foundation.

4.1 Expanding Party-Level Records

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
4.3 Creating Actor-Normalisation Functions
The event log may use different prefixes for employees, personal agents, and systems.
For example:

person:john_windward
Agent/person:john_windward
agent:person:john_windward
system:saidit
world:calendar

The following functions standardise actor identifiers, identify actor types, and generate readable chart labels.


Show the code
normalise_actor <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    str_replace(
      regex(
        "^Agent/person:",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "agent:person:"
    ) %>%
    str_replace(
      regex(
        "^agent/person:",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "agent:person:"
    ) %>%
    str_replace(
      regex(
        "^Agent:",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "agent:"
    )
}

extract_actor_type <- function(x) {
  case_when(
    str_detect(
      x,
      "^agent:person:"
    ) ~ "agent",
    str_detect(
      x,
      "^person:"
    ) ~ "person",
    str_detect(
      x,
      "^system:"
    ) ~ "system",
    str_detect(
      x,
      "^world:"
    ) ~ "world",
    str_detect(
      x,
      "^team:"
    ) ~ "team",
    str_detect(
      x,
      "^department:"
    ) ~ "department",
    str_detect(
      x,
      "^company:"
    ) ~ "company",
    TRUE ~ "other"
  )
}

format_actor_label <- function(x) {
  cleaned <- x %>%
    str_replace(
      "^agent:person:",
      ""
    ) %>%
    str_replace(
      "^person:",
      ""
    ) %>%
    str_replace(
      "^system:",
      ""
    ) %>%
    str_replace(
      "^world:",
      ""
    ) %>%
    str_replace(
      "^team:",
      ""
    ) %>%
    str_replace(
      "^department:",
      ""
    ) %>%
    str_replace(
      "^company:",
      ""
    ) %>%
    str_replace_all(
      "_",
      " "
    ) %>%
    str_to_title()

  if_else(
    str_detect(
      x,
      "^agent:person:"
    ),
    paste0(
      cleaned,
      " Agent"
    ),
    cleaned
  )
}

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
4.4 Applying Actor Normalisation
The standardisation functions are applied to each expanded party record.


Show the code
party_events_clean <- party_events %>%
  mutate(
    actor_id = normalise_actor(
      party_raw
    ),
    actor_type = extract_actor_type(
      actor_id
    ),
    actor_label = format_actor_label(
      actor_id
    )
  )

party_events_clean %>%
  select(
    event_order,
    id,
    short_name,
    timestamp_local,
    party_raw,
    actor_id,
    actor_type,
    actor_label
  ) %>%
  slice_head(

text:
6.3 Extracting Source and Target Agents
The source agent is extracted from the first personal-agent identifier in the party list.
The target agent is primarily extracted from the nested target_agent field. If this field is unavailable, the second personal-agent identifier in the party list is used as a fallback.


Show the code
suspicious_handoffs <- suspicious_instruction_events %>%
  mutate(
    agent_parties = map(
      parties,
      extract_agent_parties
    ),
    source_agent = map_chr(
      agent_parties,
      ~ dplyr::first(
        .x,
        default = NA_character_
      )
    ),
    target_agent_from_parties = map_chr(
      agent_parties,
      ~ dplyr::nth(
        .x,
        2,
        default = NA_character_
      )
    ),
    target_agent_from_details = normalise_actor(
      detail_target_agent
    ),
    target_agent = coalesce(
      target_agent_from_details,
      target_agent_from_parties
    ),
    source_label = format_actor_label(
      source_agent
    ),
    target_label = format_actor_label(
      target_agent
    ),
    self_loop = source_agent == target_agent
  ) %>%
  select(
    event_order,
    id,
    timestamp_local,
    short_name,
    file_family,
    file_path,
    source_agent,
    target_agent,
    source_label,
    target_label,
    self_loop,
    virus_flag
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    timestamp_local,
    event_order
  )

text:
6.4 Auditing Handoff Extraction Quality
The extracted handoff table is checked for duplicated event IDs, missing source agents, missing target agents, and self-loop handoffs.
A self-loop occurs when an agent delegates the suspicious task back to itself. These events may indicate repeated or inefficient task propagation.


Show the code
handoff_quality_summary <- suspicious_handoffs %>%
  summarise(
    total_handoffs = n(),
    unique_event_ids = n_distinct(
      id
    ),
    duplicate_event_ids = n() - n_distinct(
      id
    ),
    missing_source_agents = sum(
      is.na(
        source_agent
      )
    ),
    missing_target_agents = sum(
      is.na(
        target_agent
      )
    ),
    self_loop_handoffs = sum(
      self_loop,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
6.6 Creating Suspicious-Chain Summary Statistics
The three suspicious file families are compared using:

total number of handoffs;
number of unique agents;
number of self-loops;
first observed handoff;
last observed handoff;
propagation duration.



Show the code
suspicious_chain_summary <- suspicious_handoffs %>%
  group_by(
    file_family
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    handoff_count = n(),
    unique_agents = n_distinct(
      c(
        source_agent,
        target_agent
      ),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    self_loop_count = sum(
      self_loop,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    first_seen = min(
      timestamp_local,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    last_seen = max(
      timestamp_local,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    duration_hours = as.numeric(
      difftime(
        last_seen,
        first_seen,
        units = "hours"
      )
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    first_seen
  )

6.8 Creating a Repeated-Agent Summary
Some personal agents appear repeatedly across suspicious propagation chains.
The following table measures:

the number of suspicious-chain participations;
the number of distinct file families involving each agent;
the number of appearances as a source agent;
the number of appearances as a target agent.



Show the code

  transmute(
    file_family,
    agent_id = source_agent,
    agent_label = source_label,
    role = "Source"
  )

target_agent_summary <- suspicious_handoffs %>%
  transmute(
    file_family,
    agent_id = target_agent,
    agent_label = target_label,
    role = "Target"
  )

repeated_agent_summary <- bind_rows(
  source_agent_summary,
  target_agent_summary
) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(
      agent_id
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(
    agent_id,
    agent_label
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    suspicious_participations = n(),
    number_of_file_families = n_distinct(
      file_family
    ),
    source_appearances = sum(
      role == "Source"
    ),
    target_appearances = sum(
      role == "Target"
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    desc(
      number_of_file_families
    ),
    desc(
      suspicious_participations
    )
  )

WarningKey Incident Evidence



The final SwiftWren handoffs reveal a clear propagation path immediately before the anomalous SaidIT post:
Daniel Gangway Agent → Chloe Ballast Agent → John Windward Agent
The event log also confirms that:

the final delegated task was linked to SwiftWren_further_instructions.md;
the public SaidIT post used SwiftWren.txt as its content source;
SwiftWren_further_instructions.md and SwiftWren.txt were deleted immediately after the post.

These records support the conclusion that the anomalous public release was the visible endpoint of a longer instruction-file propagation chain rather than an isolated posting error.








NotePart 5 Output



This section reconstructs suspicious instruction-file handoffs at the personal-agent level.
Three recurring file families are identified: HiddenOrca, MellowOtter, and SwiftWren. The extracted handoff table records the source agent, target agent, timestamp, file family, and self-loop status for each propagation event.
The handoff-quality audit confirms that the extracted records are structurally complete. The latest SwiftWren chain is isolated for detailed review because it contains substantially more propagation events than the earlier chains.
The final posting window will be used in the next section to reconstruct the exact sequence that led to the anomalous SaidIT post.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
7.2 Preparing the Historical Comparison Table
The three suspicious chains are compared across four indicators:

handoff count;
number of unique agents;
self-loop count;
propagation duration in hours.

The comparison table is converted into a long format to support faceted visualisation.


Show the code
historical_comparison_long <- suspicious_chain_summary %>%
  select(
    file_family,
    handoff_count,
    unique_agents,
    self_loop_count,
    duration_hours
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      handoff_count,
      unique_agents,
      self_loop_count,
      duration_hours
    ),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      "handoff_count" = "Handoff Count",
      "unique_agents" = "Unique Agents",
      "self_loop_count" = "Self-Loops",
      "duration_hours" = "Duration in Hours"
    ),
    file_family = factor(
      file_family,
      levels = c(
        "HiddenOrca",
        "MellowOtter",
        "SwiftWren"

    ),
    latest_incident = file_family == "SwiftWren"

The faceted bar chart compares the three suspicious instruction-file families.

The network-node table distinguishes ordinary agents, selected critical agents, and the external SaidIT endpoint.

  swiftwren_network_edges %>%

      node_id = target_agent,
      node_label = target_label
    )
) %>%
  distinct(
    node_id,
    .keep_all = TRUE
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    node_role = case_when(
      node_id == "system:saidit" ~
        "External Platform",
      node_id %in% c(
        "agent:person:john_windward",
        "agent:person:chloe_ballast",
        "agent:person:daniel_gangway"
      ) ~
        "Critical Agent",
      TRUE ~
        "Other Agent"
    ),
    display_label = case_when(
      node_id %in% c(
        "agent:person:john_windward",
        "agent:person:chloe_ballast",
        "agent:person:daniel_gangway",
        "system:saidit",
        "agent:person:emma_harbor"
      ) ~
        node_label,
      TRUE ~
        NA_character_
    )
  )

7.10 Creating the SwiftWren Directed Graph
The static graph object is created using tidygraph.
Degree and betweenness centrality are calculated to support later interpretation.


Show the code
swiftwren_graph <- tbl_graph(
  nodes = swiftwren_network_nodes,
  edges = swiftwren_network_edges %>%
    select(
      source_agent,
      target_agent,
      handoff_count,
      edge_type
    ),
  directed = TRUE
) %>%
  activate(
    nodes
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    in_degree = centrality_degree(
      mode = "in"
    ),
    out_degree = centrality_degree(
      mode = "out"
    ),
    total_degree = centrality_degree(
      mode = "all"
    ),
    betweenness = centrality_betweenness(
      directed = TRUE
    )
  )

text:
7.11 Visualising the SwiftWren Propagation Network
The static network shows the main structure of the SwiftWren chain.
Node size represents the total number of direct network connections. Critical agents and the external SaidIT endpoint are highlighted.


Show the code
set.seed(
  1234
)

ggraph(
  swiftwren_graph,
  layout = "stress"
) +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(
      width = handoff_count,
      color = edge_type
    ),
    alpha = 0.32,
    arrow = grid::arrow(
      length = grid::unit(
        2.2,
        "mm"
      ),
      type = "closed"
    ),
    end_cap = circle(
      2.6,
      "mm"
    ),
    show.legend = TRUE
  ) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(
      size = total_degree,
      color = node_role
    ),
    alpha = 0.95
  ) +
  geom_node_text(
    aes(
      label = display_label
    ),
    repel = TRUE,
    size = 3.6,
    fontface = "bold",
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(
    range = c(
      0.25,
      1.8
    )
  ) +
  scale_edge_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Agent Handoff" = "#AAB7B8",
      "Public Post" = "#E76F51"
    )
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Other Agent" = "#85C1E9",
      "Critical Agent" = "#F5B041",
      "External Platform" = "#E76F51"
    )
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(
      3,
      9
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "SwiftWren Agent-to-Agent Propagation Network",
    subtitle = "Selected labels highlight the final path leading to the SaidIT endpoint",
    size = "Total Degree",
    color = "Node Role",
    edge_color = "Edge Type",
    edge_width = "Handoff Count"
  ) +
  theme_graph(
    base_family = "sans"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right"
  )









The SwiftWren propagation network shows that the anomalous public post was not an isolated action. The suspicious instruction file circulated through a dense agent-to-agent network before reaching John Windward Agent. The highlighted path shows that Daniel Gangway Agent and Chloe Ballast Agent were involved shortly before the final handoff to John Windward Agent. The final public-post edge then connects John Windward Agent to SaidIT.

text:
7.13 Creating the Final Incident Timeline
The final incident timeline focuses on the actions most directly related to public release.
The relevant events include:

the final SwiftWren instruction handoff;
the SaidIT pre-post check;
the public SaidIT post;
deletion of the related instruction and content files.



Show the code
final_incident_timeline <- events_enriched %>%
  filter(
    timestamp_local >= incident_time_local - minutes(
      10
    ),
    timestamp_local <= incident_time_local + minutes(
      5
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    event_group = case_when(
      short_name == "queue_subordinate_task" &
        str_detect(
          coalesce(
            file_path,
            ""
          ),
          "SwiftWren_further_instructions\\.md"
        ) ~
        "Instruction Handoff",
      short_name == "saidit_post_check" ~
        "Pre-Post Check",
      short_name == "saidit_post" ~
        "Public SaidIT Post",
      short_name == "delete_file" &
        detail_target %in% c(
          "SwiftWren_further_instructions.md",
          "SwiftWren.txt"
        ) ~
        "File Deletion",
      TRUE ~
        "Other Activity"
    ),
    event_description = case_when(
      timestamp_local == ymd_hms(
        "2046-05-17 04:12:24",
        tz = "America/Los_Angeles"
      ) ~
        "Daniel Gangway → Chloe Ballast",
      timestamp_local == ymd_hms(
        "2046-05-17 04:21:13",
        tz = "America/Los_Angeles"
      ) ~
        "Chloe Ballast → John Windward",
      event_group == "Pre-Post Check" ~
        "SaidIT pre-post check",
      event_group == "Public SaidIT Post" ~
        "Published SwiftWren.txt",
      event_group == "File Deletion" &
        detail_target == "SwiftWren_further_instructions.md" ~
        "Deleted instruction file",
      event_group == "File Deletion" &
        detail_target == "SwiftWren.txt" ~
        "Deleted content file",
      TRUE ~
        short_name
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    event_group != "Other Activity"

  select(
    timestamp_local,

WarningKey Visual Analytics Findings



The visual evidence identifies a recurring suspicious instruction-file propagation pattern.

HiddenOrca, MellowOtter, and SwiftWren exhibit similar handoff behaviour.
SwiftWren is the largest and most persistent chain.
The latest chain reaches John Windward Agent shortly before the public SaidIT post.
The post uses SwiftWren.txt as its confirmed content source.
The related instruction and content files are deleted immediately after release.

The available evidence links the public release to John Windward Agent. The logs do not establish that John Windward personally authored or manually submitted the anomalous content.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
8.1 Investigation Scope
The previous section reconstructs the propagation chain that led to the anomalous SaidIT post. This section focuses on the origin of the public-post content and examines whether similar public-release patterns occurred historically.
The analysis distinguishes between two forms of evidence:

confirmed evidence, which is directly recorded in the event log;
remaining uncertainty, which cannot be resolved because the full text contents of the suspicious files may not be available in the dataset.

This distinction is important because the event log can establish the operational pathway of the post without necessarily revealing the complete semantic meaning of the underlying text.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
8.3 Reviewing SaidIT Posting Events
The event log is filtered to identify all SaidIT posting events.
Selected nested fields are extracted to determine:

the posting timestamp;
the actors involved;
the forum destination;
the content source;
whether the content source belongs to a suspicious file family.

  filter(
    short_name == "saidit_post"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    parties_display = map_chr(
      parties,
      ~ paste(
        .x,
        collapse = ", "
      )
    ),
    detail_forum = map_chr(
      details,
      ~ pluck_chr(
        .x,
        "forum"
      )
    ),
    content_family = str_remove(
      detail_content_source,
      "\\.txt$"

    suspicious_content_source = content_family %in%

    event_order,

    timestamp_local,

    detail_forum,
    detail_content_source,
    content_family,

  ) %>%
  filter(
    str_detect(
      details_text,
      "HiddenOrca|MellowOtter|SwiftWren"
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    possible_saved_content = map_chr(
      details,
      ~ first_non_missing_chr(
        pluck_chr(
          .x,
          "content"
        ),
        pluck_chr(
          .x,
          "text"
        ),
        pluck_chr(
          .x,
          "message"
        ),
        pluck_chr(
          .x,
          "body"
        )
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    event_order,
    id,
    timestamp_local,
    short_name,
    possible_saved_content
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(
      possible_saved_content

  )

The SaidIT log contains 108 public posts. Among them, 105 posts store embedded text directly in the content field. Only three posts do not contain embedded text. These three records instead reference external content-source files: HiddenOrca.txt, MellowOtter.txt, and SwiftWren.txt.
This structural difference distinguishes the suspicious posts from ordinary SaidIT activity. The event log confirms the source filenames, but it does not preserve the full text contents of the three suspicious files.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
8.9 Extracting Suspicious Pre-Post Checks
The historical evidence suggests that the suspicious SaidIT posts were not released immediately without validation. Each suspicious post was preceded by a saidit_post_check event.
However, the pre-post check records do not directly contain the associated suspicious file-family name. Therefore, each suspicious public post is matched to the nearest pre-post check occurring within the previous five seconds.


Show the code
saidit_pre_post_checks <- events_enriched %>%
  filter(
    short_name == "saidit_post_check"
  ) %>%
  select(
    check_event_order = event_order,
    check_id = id,
    check_time = timestamp_local,
    check_parties = parties
  )

suspicious_pre_post_checks <- suspicious_saidit_posts %>%
  transmute(
    file_family = content_family,
    post_id = id,
    post_time = timestamp_local
  ) %>%
  inner_join(
    saidit_pre_post_checks,
    by = character(),
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    seconds_before_post = as.numeric(
      difftime(
        post_time,
        check_time,
        units = "secs"
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    seconds_before_post >= 0,
    seconds_before_post <= 5
  ) %>%
  group_by(
    file_family,
    post_id
  ) %>%
  slice_min(
    order_by = seconds_before_post,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(
    post_time
  )

This is an important finding. The validation process was present, but it did not prevent the release of any suspicious post.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
8.10 Extracting Suspicious File-Deletion Events
The analysis next identifies file-deletion events associated with the three suspicious file families.
Both the _further_instructions.md files and the corresponding .txt content files are included. These events are relevant because the files were deleted immediately after public release.


Show the code
suspicious_file_deletions <- events_enriched %>%
  filter(
    short_name == "delete_file"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    deleted_file = coalesce(
      detail_target,
      detail_file,
      file_path
    ),
    file_family = case_when(
      str_detect(
        coalesce(
          deleted_file,
          ""
        ),
        "_further_instructions\\.md$"
      ) ~
        str_remove(
          deleted_file,
          "_further_instructions\\.md$"
        ),
      str_detect(
        coalesce(
          deleted_file,
          ""
        ),
        "\\.txt$"
      ) ~
        str_remove(
          deleted_file,
          "\\.txt$"
        ),
      TRUE ~
        NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    file_family %in%
      suspicious_file_families
  ) %>%
  select(
    event_order,
    id,
    timestamp_local,
    file_family,
    deleted_file
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    timestamp_local,
    event_order
  )

section: 8.11 Preparing the Corrected Historical Evidence Matrix
text:
8.11 Preparing the Corrected Historical Evidence Matrix
The historical evidence matrix compares whether each suspicious file family contains four stages:

instruction-file handoff;
SaidIT pre-post check;
public SaidIT post;
file deletion.

The matrix is constructed from the corrected event tables rather than relying on direct file-name matching within the pre-post check records.


Show the code
handoff_evidence <- suspicious_handoffs %>%
  distinct(
    file_family
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    file_family,
    event_stage = "Instruction Handoff"
  )

pre_post_check_evidence <- suspicious_pre_post_checks %>%
  distinct(
    file_family
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    file_family,
    event_stage = "Pre-Post Check"
  )

public_post_evidence <- suspicious_saidit_posts %>%
  distinct(
    content_family
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    file_family = content_family,
    event_stage = "Public SaidIT Post"
  )

file_deletion_evidence <- suspicious_file_deletions %>%
  distinct(
    file_family
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    file_family,
    event_stage = "File Deletion"
  )

historical_evidence_matrix <- bind_rows(
  handoff_evidence,
  pre_post_check_evidence,
  public_post_evidence,
  file_deletion_evidence
) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  mutate(
    observed = TRUE
  ) %>%
  complete(
    file_family = suspicious_file_families,
    event_stage = c(
      "Instruction Handoff",
      "Pre-Post Check",
      "Public SaidIT Post",
      "File Deletion"
    ),
    fill = list(
      observed = FALSE
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = event_stage,
    values_from = observed,
    values_fill = FALSE
  )

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
9.1 Selecting One Intervention Point
The historical analysis identifies a recurring four-stage pattern:

suspicious instruction-file handoffs;
a SaidIT pre-post check;
a public SaidIT post using an external content-source file; and
immediate deletion of the related files.

The three suspicious posts all passed through an existing SaidIT pre-post check exactly one second before public release. However, the current check did not prevent publication.
This report recommends strengthening one intervention point:

The SaidIT pre-post validation gate immediately before public release.

This location is selected because every public SaidIT post must pass through the same gateway. Upstream agent-to-agent handoffs may follow different routes, involve different actors, or change over time. In contrast, the final posting gateway is a consistent control point.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
9.2 Defining the Proposed Validation Logic
The proposed control uses a transparent rule-based design.
A SaidIT post should be routed to human review when it uses an external content-source file rather than embedded text. The validation gate should also record whether the external file belongs to a family associated with instruction-file propagation.
The initial rule is deliberately simple:
If a SaidIT post uses an external content-source file:
    Block direct publication
    Route the post to human review
Otherwise:
    Allow the standard publication workflow
This rule is explainable and directly supported by the historical evidence. Among the 108 SaidIT posts, 105 contain embedded text. Only three use external content-source files. These three records correspond exactly to HiddenOrca.txt, MellowOtter.txt, and SwiftWren.txt.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
9.3 Creating a Post-Level Validation Dataset
The SaidIT posting events are converted into a validation table.
The table records:

whether embedded text is available;
whether an external content-source file is used;
the associated file family;
whether the file family is linked to suspicious instruction-file propagation;
whether the proposed control would route the post to human review.



Show the code
saidit_validation_dataset <- events_enriched %>%
  filter(
    short_name == "saidit_post"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    parties_display = map_chr(
      parties,
      ~ paste(
        .x,
        collapse = ", "
      )
    ),
    embedded_text = map_chr(
      details,
      ~ first_non_missing_chr(
        pluck_chr(
          .x,
          "content"
        ),
        pluck_chr(
          .x,
          "text"
        ),
        pluck_chr(
          .x,
          "message"
        ),
        pluck_chr(
          .x,
          "body"
        ),
        pluck_chr(
          .x,
          "post"
        )
      )
    ),
    external_content_source = !is.na(
      detail_content_source
    ),
    content_family = str_remove(
      detail_content_source,
      "\\.txt$"
    ),
    linked_instruction_chain = content_family %in%
      suspicious_file_families,
    proposed_action = if_else(
      external_content_source,
      "Route to Human Review",
      "Allow Standard Workflow"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    event_order,
    id,
    timestamp_local,
    parties_display,
    embedded_text,
    detail_content_source,
    content_family,
    external_content_source,
    linked_instruction_chain,
    proposed_action
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    timestamp_local,
    event_order
  )

title: Take-Home_Ex02
section: 9.11 Why This Intervention Point Is Effective
text:
9.11 Why This Intervention Point Is Effective
The proposed pre-post validation gate is selected for three reasons.

Consistent control location
Agent-to-agent propagation paths are complex and may change over time. The SwiftWren chain alone contains 186 handoffs involving 18 agents. A control placed at one upstream agent would not reliably block future variants.
In contrast, all public SaidIT posts must pass through the same posting gateway.


Strong historical signal
The event log contains 108 SaidIT posts. Among them, 105 store embedded text directly. Only three posts use external content-source files. These three records correspond exactly to the suspicious HiddenOrca, MellowOtter, and SwiftWren incidents.


Limited operational burden
The proposed rule routes only external-file posts to human review. Standard posts with embedded text continue through the existing workflow.
This design improves safety without requiring manual review of every ordinary SaidIT post.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
10.5 Answering the Analytical Questions

How was the anomalous SaidIT post generated?
The event log shows that the anomalous SwiftWren post was the final outcome of a longer instruction-file propagation chain.
The last observed handoffs were:
Daniel Gangway Agent
→ Chloe Ballast Agent
→ John Windward Agent
John Windward Agent then passed through a SaidIT pre-post check. One second later, the public SaidIT post was released using SwiftWren.txt as its content source. The related instruction and content files were deleted immediately after release.


What was the origin of the post content?
The event log confirms that the anomalous public post used:
SwiftWren.txt
as its content source.
The suspicious file was linked to:
SwiftWren_further_instructions.md
which circulated through the personal-agent network before the public release.
The full text content of the suspicious external files is not preserved in the available event records. Therefore, the operational origin of the post can be identified, but its complete semantic meaning cannot be conclusively reconstructed.


Were there earlier warning signs?
Yes.
Two earlier file families followed the same operational pattern:
HiddenOrca
MellowOtter
Each historical incident involved:

repeated instruction-file handoffs;
a SaidIT pre-post check;
a public post using an external content-source file; and
immediate deletion of the related files.

The earlier incidents should therefore be interpreted as warning signals rather than unrelated anomalies.


Where should the system intervene?
The recommended intervention point is the SaidIT pre-post validation gate.
Any agent-generated post referencing an external content-source file should be blocked from direct publication and routed to human review.
This control point is preferable to a rule targeting one upstream agent because propagation routes may change. In contrast, every public SaidIT post must pass through the final posting gateway.






ImportantMain Analytical Conclusion



The latest SwiftWren event was not an isolated malfunction.
The evidence reveals a recurring instruction-file propagation pattern across HiddenOrca, MellowOtter, and SwiftWren. All three incidents passed through the existing SaidIT pre-post check, produced a public post using an external content-source file, and were followed by immediate deletion of the related files.
The recommended intervention is a strengthened SaidIT pre-post validation gate that blocks direct publication of external-file posts and routes them to human review.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
11.1 Evidence Boundaries
The investigation identifies a clear operational pathway, but several limitations remain.

The full suspicious-file contents are unavailable
The event log confirms that the three suspicious posts used:
HiddenOrca.txt
MellowOtter.txt
SwiftWren.txt
as external content-source files.
However, the full contents of these files are not preserved in the available records. The report can identify the content origin but cannot conclusively interpret the complete semantic meaning of each post.


Human intent cannot be established
The public releases are linked to:
John Windward Agent
The available logs do not establish that John Windward personally authored, approved, or manually submitted the suspicious posts.
The analysis therefore identifies an agent-system failure pathway rather than proving deliberate human misconduct.


Historical backtesting does not guarantee future performance
The proposed validation rule retrospectively identifies all three historical suspicious releases.
However, future unsafe behaviours may differ from the observed pattern. For example, a future agent may embed suspicious text directly rather than reference an external file.
The rule should be treated as an effective first-line control rather than a complete security solution.


Network centrality does not prove causality
Several personal agents appear frequently within the suspicious propagation chains. Their high participation counts and network positions identify operational exposure, but they do not prove that those agents originated the unsafe instructions.


Legitimate external-file posts may exist
The available dataset shows that all three observed external-file posts were suspicious. In a larger production environment, legitimate use cases may also exist.
Human-review procedures should therefore be designed with clear response-time standards and audit requirements.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
Take-Home_Ex01
text:
Motor insurance is one of the major business lines in the general insurance industry. For insurers, portfolio profitability depends not only on the amount of premium collected, but also on the frequency and severity of claims. Even when the overall portfolio appears profitable, certain policyholder, vehicle, or policy segments may still generate high losses and create volatility.
In practice, insurers need to identify which customer, vehicle, and policy characteristics are associated with higher claim costs and lower profitability. Visual analytics provides a useful approach because it combines data visualization, statistical summaries, and exploratory analysis to reveal patterns that may not be obvious from aggregate figures alone.
Therefore, this study applies visual analytics techniques to a motor insurance portfolio dataset to investigate profitability, claim volatility, and high-risk segments.



The objective of this take-home exercise is to use appropriate visual analytics methods, tidyverse functions, and ggplot2 extensions to explore the profitability and volatility of a motor insurance portfolio.
Specifically, this report aims to answer the following analytically questions:

What are the distributions of premium income, claim cost, claim frequency, and loss ratio in the insurance portfolio?
How does portfolio profitability change across years?
Is weak profitability mainly driven by claim frequency, claim severity, or pricing inadequacy?
Which policy characteristics, such as policy type, policy status, business type, and payment frequency, are associated with higher loss ratios?
Which vehicle and driver characteristics, such as fuel type, driver age, vehicle age, and vehicle value, are associated with higher claim risk?
Are the observed visual patterns statistically supported by validation methods?

Based on the analysis, this report provides practical insights that may support insurance pricing, underwriting, and portfolio management decisions.







pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  janitor,
  scales,
  ggthemes,
  plotly,
  DT,
  broom,
  DiagrammeR
)

theme_set(theme_minimal())

The tidyverse family of packages is used for data importing, wrangling, transformation, and visualization. The janitor package is used to standardize column names and check data quality. The scales package is used to format percentage and currency values in charts. The plot package is used to create an interactive visualization as an extension of ggplot2. The broom package is used to present model outputs in a tidy format.



The dataset used in this study is a real-world motor vehicle insurance portfolio dataset from a Spanish insurance company specialized in non-life insurance. The dataset contains policy-level information, including policy characteristics, driver characteristics, vehicle characteristics, premium income, claim counts, claim costs, and exposure.
The main variables used in this analysis include total premium, total incurred claims, total claims, total exposure, policy type, policy status, payment frequency, driver age, vehicle age, fuel type, vehicle value, and circulation area.

Several analytically variables are created to support the insurance portfolio analysis. Profit is calculated as total premium minus total incurred claims. Loss ratio is calculated as total incurred claims divided by total premium and is used as the main profitability measure. A higher loss ratio indicates weaker profitability.
Claim frequency is calculated as total claims divided by total exposure, while claim severity is calculated as total incurred claims divided by total claims. These two variables help distinguish whether poor portfolio performance is driven by frequent claims or by large claim amounts.

This section examines the distribution of claim costs and loss ratios to understand portfolio volatility. Insurance claim data are usually highly skewed because most policies have no or small claims, while a small number of policies generate very large losses. Therefore, distributional visualisation is important before conducting segment-level analysis.
The filter() function is used to focus on policies with positive incurred claims where appropriate. The geom_histogram() function is used to visualise claim cost and loss ratio distributions. For total incurred claims, scale_x_log10() is applied because the original claim amount distribution is highly right-skewed. A claim concentration curve is also created to assess whether a small share of high-loss policies accounts for a large share of total incurred claims.

This section extends the analysis beyond one-variable bar charts by using advanced visual analytics techniques. The purpose is to identify high-risk segment combinations and to provide a more interactive view of portfolio performance.
A heatmap is used to combine policy type and payment frequency in one visualisation. This helps identify whether high loss ratios are concentrated in specific product-payment combinations. A quadrant chart is then used to compare claim frequency and loss ratio at the same time, with bubble size representing premium volume. The risk heatmap is created by grouping the data by policy type and payment frequency. The geom_tile() function is used to display each segment as a cell, while fill colour represents the segment-level loss ratio. The geom_text() function is used to place the loss ratio value inside each cell.
This visual design is useful because it allows two categorical variables to be examined simultaneously. It can reveal high-risk combinations that may be hidden when policy type and payment frequency are analysed separately.

The interactive visualisation is created using ggplotly() from the plotly package. The original ggplot object is converted into an interactive chart, allowing users to hover over each point and inspect detailed information such as loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, premium income, and profit.
This is useful for exploratory visual analytics because insurance portfolio review often requires comparing multiple performance indicators at the same time. The interactive chart allows users to move from a broad visual pattern to detailed segment-level information.

The plotThe Code











interactive_policy_plot <- ggplot(
  policy_type_summary,
  aes(
    x = claim_frequency,
    y = loss_ratio,
    size = premium,
    text = paste(
      "Policy Type:", policy_type,
      "<br>Loss Ratio:", percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1),
      "<br>Claim Frequency:", round(claim_frequency, 3),
      "<br>Claim Severity:", dollar(claim_severity),
      "<br>Premium:", dollar(premium),
      "<br>Profit:", dollar(profit)
    )
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.75,
    color = "#2C7FB8"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = policy_type),
    vjust = -1,
    size = 3.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = portfolio_summary$overall_loss_ratio,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = portfolio_summary$overall_claim_frequency,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent,
    limits = c(0.50, 1.00)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, max(policy_type_summary$claim_frequency) * 1.15)
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  labs(
    title = "Interactive Segment Analysis by Policy Type",

    x = "Claim Frequency",
    y = "Loss Ratio",
    size = "Premium"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(interactive_policy_plot, tooltip = "text")




The interactive segment-level visualisation extends the premium adequacy quadrant by allowing users to inspect each policy type directly. Each point represents one policy type. The x-axis shows claim frequency, the y-axis shows loss ratio, and the bubble size represents premium volume. When the user hovers over a point, the tooltip displays additional information, including loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, premium income, and profit.
This interactive design is useful because insurance portfolio review often requires comparing multiple indicators at the same time. A static chart can show the overall pattern, but an interactive chart allows decision-makers to examine the details of each segment more efficiently. For example, COMP_E has a loss ratio of 73.9%, claim frequency of 0.41, claim severity of about $990, premium income of about $35.3 million, and profit of about $9.2 million. This helps show that although COMP_E has weaker-than-average profitability, it still contributes positive underwriting profit.
From a visual analytics perspective, the interactive chart supports deeper exploration beyond dashboard reporting. It allows the analyst to move from a broad pattern to specific segment details. This is especially useful for identifying policy types that combine high premium volume, high claim frequency, and weak profitability. These segments should be prioritised for pricing review, underwriting refinement, or further claim driver investigation.
Overall, the interactive chart confirms that COMP_N is the most concerning policy type because it is located in the high-frequency and high-loss-ratio area. It also shows that some policy types with weaker profitability still generate positive profit because of their premium volume. Therefore, interactive visual analytics helps balance risk, profitability, and business scale in portfolio review.




The risk heatmap reveals that profitability problems are concentrated in specific product-payment combinations.
The premium adequacy quadrant confirms that COMP_N is located in the high-frequency and high-loss-ratio area.
The interactive visualisation allows users to inspect loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, premium volume, and profit at the same time.
Together, these advanced visualisations move the analysis beyond simple dashboard reporting and provide more actionable support for pricing and underwriting review.







The previous sections used visual analytics to identify important patterns in the insurance portfolio. However, visual patterns alone may be influenced by skewed distributions, uneven sample sizes, or random variation. Therefore, statistical validation is used to support the main visual findings.
The purpose of these tests is not to replace the visual analysis, but to check whether the observed relationships are statistically meaningful. Since insurance variables such as loss ratio and claim cost are highly skewed, non-parametric and categorical tests are used where appropriate.




kruskal_policy <- kruskal.test(loss_ratio ~ policy_type, data = motor_clean)

kruskal_policy

  test = "Kruskal-Wallis test",

A Kruskal-Wallis test is used to examine whether the distribution of loss ratio differs across policy types. This test is selected because loss ratio is highly skewed and does not necessarily satisfy the normality assumption required by a standard ANOVA.
The visual analysis showed that COMP_N has the highest loss ratio among all policy types, while TP has the lowest. The Kruskal-Wallis test provides statistical support for this pattern. If the p-value is statistically significant, it suggests that profitability differs across policy types and that the differences shown in the visualisation are unlikely to be due only to random variation.
This result supports the earlier finding that policy type is an important driver of portfolio profitability. In particular, COMP_N should be treated as a priority segment because it combines the highest loss ratio with the highest claim frequency.

A logistic regression model is used as a supporting validation method for claim occurrence. The model estimates whether selected driver, vehicle, and policy characteristics are associated with the probability of having at least one claim after controlling for other variables.
Because the full dataset is large, a random sample of 50,000 observations is used for this validation model. The purpose of the model is not to build a full predictive model, but to support the visual analytics findings. The output is reported using odds ratios. An odds ratio above 1 indicates higher odds of having a claim, while an odds ratio below 1 indicates lower odds of having a claim.
This model helps check whether the visual findings remain meaningful when several variables are analysed together. For example, if policy type, fuel type, or payment frequency remains statistically significant, it supports the earlier segment-level findings that these variables are associated with claim risk.




The visual analytics reveal several important findings about the motor insurance portfolio.
First, the portfolio is profitable overall, but profitability deteriorates over time. The yearly loss ratio increased from 65.7% in 2022 to 66.5% in 2023 and then to 74.7% in 2024. Although the loss ratio remains below the 100% break-even threshold, the upward trend indicates that the underwriting margin became thinner in 2024.
Second, both premium income and incurred claims increased from 2022 to 2024. However, incurred claims grew faster relative to premium income, especially in 2024. This explains why the portfolio loss ratio increased. Business growth alone does not guarantee stronger profitability if claim costs grow faster than premium income.
Third, claim costs are highly concentrated. The claim concentration curve shows that a small share of high-loss policies contributes a large share of total incurred claims. This means that portfolio volatility is strongly influenced by tail-risk observations rather than only by average claim behaviour.
Fourth, the frequency-severity decomposition shows that claim frequency increased steadily from 2022 to 2024, while claim severity decreased in 2023 but rebounded in 2024. Therefore, the deterioration in 2024 profitability appears to be driven by both higher claim frequency and a rebound in average claim size.
Fifth, policy type is a major driver of profitability. COMP_N has the highest loss ratio at 93.5% and the highest claim frequency at 1.04. This makes COMP_N the most concerning policy type because it combines weak profitability with frequent claim occurrence.
Sixth, policy status is strongly associated with profitability. Policy status C has a loss ratio of 128.0%, which is above the 100% break-even threshold. This means that claim costs exceed premium income for this segment. In contrast, policy status A has a much lower loss ratio of 64.5%.
Seventh, payment frequency is associated with different profitability patterns. Annual payment policies have the lowest loss ratio at 67.9%, while quarterly and semi-annual payment policies have higher loss ratios of 76.4% and 80.7%, respectively. This suggests that non-annual payment groups may have weaker profitability.
Eighth, diesel vehicles show weaker profitability than gasoline vehicles, but the difference is mainly frequency-driven. Diesel vehicles have a higher claim frequency of 0.342 compared with 0.246 for gasoline vehicles. However, claim severity is almost identical between the two groups, at approximately $959 for diesel vehicles and $960 for gasoline vehicles. This suggests that diesel vehicles do not generate more expensive claims on average; instead, they generate claims more often.
Ninth, driver age and vehicle age show non-linear profitability patterns. For driver age, the 26–35, 36–45, and 66+ groups have relatively higher loss ratios, while the 18–25 group has the lowest loss ratio. For vehicle age, the 0–5 and 11–20 groups show weaker profitability than older vehicle groups.
Finally, the advanced visual analytics reveal more specific high-risk combinations. The risk heatmap shows that COMP_N policies with semi-annual payment have a loss ratio of 108.8%, making this segment loss-making. The premium adequacy quadrant also confirms that COMP_N is located in the high-frequency and high-loss-ratio area.



The findings provide several practical implications for insurance portfolio management.
First, COMP_N should be prioritised for pricing and underwriting review. It has the highest loss ratio and the highest claim frequency among all policy types. This suggests that the premium charged for COMP_N may not fully reflect its claim occurrence risk. The insurer should further examine the customer profile, vehicle characteristics, coverage design, and underwriting rules associated with this policy type.
Second, the insurer should pay particular attention to COMP_N policies with semi-annual payment frequency. The risk heatmap shows that this specific segment has a loss ratio of 108.8%, which means it is loss-making. This finding shows the value of segment-level visual analytics. The problem is not only COMP_N as a broad policy type, but more specifically COMP_N combined with semi-annual payment.
Third, policy status C requires further investigation. Its loss ratio is 128.0%, which means claim costs exceed premium income. The insurer should examine whether policy closure or cancellation is related to adverse claim experience. If customers with poor claim experience are more likely to enter status C, this may indicate retention risk or adverse selection.
Fourth, the rising yearly loss ratio suggests that the insurer should monitor pricing adequacy over time. The portfolio remains profitable, but the margin of profitability became smaller in 2024. If claim frequency or claim severity continues to increase, premium adjustments or underwriting refinements may be necessary.
Fifth, the claim concentration result suggests that tail-risk monitoring should be included in regular portfolio review. A small number of large-loss policies can have a significant effect on total incurred claims. Therefore, large-loss policies should be analysed separately to identify whether they are concentrated in specific policy types, vehicle age groups, fuel types, or payment frequency groups.
Sixth, diesel vehicles should be monitored as a frequency-driven risk segment. The analysis shows that diesel vehicles have higher claim frequency and higher loss ratio than gasoline vehicles, while claim severity is almost the same. This means the insurer should investigate vehicle usage intensity, customer driving patterns, exposure characteristics, or policy type composition for diesel vehicles, rather than focusing only on repair cost per claim.
Finally, non-annual payment groups should also be monitored as potential risk indicators. Quarterly and semi-annual payment groups have higher loss ratios than annual payment policies. This result should not be interpreted as causal evidence, but it provides a useful segmentation signal for further underwriting and pricing investigation.



This study has several limitations.
First, the analysis is exploratory and focuses on associations rather than causal effects. For example, the finding that COMP_N has a higher loss ratio does not prove that the policy type itself causes higher claims. The result may also reflect differences in customer profiles, vehicle characteristics, coverage design, or exposure patterns.
Second, some variables are coded categories and require deeper business interpretation. Without full internal documentation from the insurer, the exact business meaning of some categories may not be fully clear.
Third, the dataset does not include external factors such as repair cost inflation, regional traffic density, weather conditions, fraud risk, or macroeconomic conditions. These external factors may also affect claim frequency and claim severity.
Fourth, the logistic regression model is used only as a supporting validation method. It is not intended to be a full predictive model. A more advanced predictive modelling framework could be developed in future work to estimate claim probability, claim severity, or expected loss more accurately.
Finally, some charts aggregate policies into broad groups, such as driver age groups and vehicle age groups. While grouping improves readability, it may hide variation within each group.



In conclusion, this take-home exercise demonstrates how visual analytics can be used to investigate profitability, claim volatility, and high-risk segments in a motor insurance portfolio.
The analysis shows that the portfolio is profitable overall, but profitability deteriorated from 2022 to 2024. The loss ratio increased to 74.7% in 2024, indicating that claim costs became heavier relative to premium income. Frequency-severity decomposition further shows that this deterioration is related to both higher claim frequency and a rebound in claim severity.
The segment-level analysis reveals that profitability problems are not evenly distributed across the portfolio. COMP_N is the most concerning policy type because it has both the highest loss ratio and the highest claim frequency. Policy status C is also a clear loss-making segment, with a loss ratio of 128.0%. Payment frequency, driver age, vehicle age, and fuel type also provide useful segmentation signals.
The fuel type analysis shows the value of separating claim frequency from claim severity. Diesel vehicles have weaker profitability than gasoline vehicles, but their claim severity is almost identical. Their weaker performance is mainly driven by more frequent claim occurrence rather than larger individual claim costs. This demonstrates why frequency-severity decomposition is important for insurance portfolio analysis.
The advanced visual analytics provide more detailed insights. The risk heatmap identifies COMP_N with semi-annual payment as a specific loss-making segment, while the premium adequacy quadrant confirms that COMP_N is located in the high-frequency and high-loss-ratio area. The interactive chart further supports exploratory investigation by allowing users to inspect loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, premium volume, and profit at the segment level.
Overall, this report shows that visual analytics can move insurance analysis beyond simple dashboard reporting. It helps identify where profitability problems are concentrated, explains whether weak performance is frequency-driven or severity-driven, and supports more targeted underwriting, pricing, and portfolio management decisions.

title: Take-Home_Ex01
text:
Motor insurance is one of the major business lines in the general insurance industry. For insurers, portfolio profitability depends not only on the amount of premium collected, but also on the frequency and severity of claims. Even when the overall portfolio appears profitable, certain policyholder, vehicle, or policy segments may still generate high losses and create volatility.
In practice, insurers need to identify which customer, vehicle, and policy characteristics are associated with higher claim costs and lower profitability. Visual analytics provides a useful approach because it combines data visualization, statistical summaries, and exploratory analysis to reveal patterns that may not be obvious from aggregate figures alone.
Therefore, this study applies visual analytics techniques to a motor insurance portfolio dataset to investigate profitability, claim volatility, and high-risk segments.



The objective of this take-home exercise is to use appropriate visual analytics methods, tidyverse functions, and ggplot2 extensions to explore the profitability and volatility of a motor insurance portfolio.
Specifically, this report aims to answer the following analytically questions:

What are the distributions of premium income, claim cost, claim frequency, and loss ratio in the insurance portfolio?
How does portfolio profitability change across years?
Is weak profitability mainly driven by claim frequency, claim severity, or pricing inadequacy?
Which policy characteristics, such as policy type, policy status, business type, and payment frequency, are associated with higher loss ratios?
Which vehicle and driver characteristics, such as fuel type, driver age, vehicle age, and vehicle value, are associated with higher claim risk?
Are the observed visual patterns statistically supported by validation methods?

Based on the analysis, this report provides practical insights that may support insurance pricing, underwriting, and portfolio management decisions.

The tidyverse family of packages is used for data importing, wrangling, transformation, and visualization. The janitor package is used to standardize column names and check data quality. The scales package is used to format percentage and currency values in charts. The plot package is used to create an interactive visualization as an extension of ggplot2. The broom package is used to present model outputs in a tidy format.



The dataset used in this study is a real-world motor vehicle insurance portfolio dataset from a Spanish insurance company specialized in non-life insurance. The dataset contains policy-level information, including policy characteristics, driver characteristics, vehicle characteristics, premium income, claim counts, claim costs, and exposure.
The main variables used in this analysis include total premium, total incurred claims, total claims, total exposure, policy type, policy status, payment frequency, driver age, vehicle age, fuel type, vehicle value, and circulation area.

Several analytically variables are created to support the insurance portfolio analysis. Profit is calculated as total premium minus total incurred claims. Loss ratio is calculated as total incurred claims divided by total premium and is used as the main profitability measure. A higher loss ratio indicates weaker profitability.
Claim frequency is calculated as total claims divided by total exposure, while claim severity is calculated as total incurred claims divided by total claims. These two variables help distinguish whether poor portfolio performance is driven by frequent claims or by large claim amounts.

Driver age, vehicle age, and vehicle value are grouped into categorical variables. This makes the visual analysis easier to interpret and allows the report to identify segment-level risk patterns more clearly.
After the data wrangling process, the analytical dataset is ready for visual analysis. The cleaning process includes standardising column names, checking duplicates, examining missing values, removing observations with missing values in key variables, and creating insurance-specific analytical metrics.
The most important derived variables are profit, loss ratio, claim frequency, and claim severity. These variables are necessary because the original dataset only provides raw premium and claim information. By transforming the raw variables into insurance performance indicators, the analysis can evaluate not only whether the portfolio is profitable, but also why some segments are less profitable than others.
Loss ratio is used as the main profitability measure. Claim frequency and claim severity are used to decompose claim risk into two components: how often claims occur and how expensive each claim is. This distinction is important because two segments may have similar loss ratios but very different risk structures.









The analytical workflow map summarises how the raw motor insurance portfolio dataset is transformed into a visual analytics report. The process begins with data wrangling, including column name cleaning, duplicate checking, missing value checking, and removal of missing observations in key variables.
After cleaning the data, several insurance-specific metrics are created, including profit, loss ratio, claim frequency, and claim severity. These variables are central to the analysis because they allow the report to evaluate not only whether the portfolio is profitable, but also whether weak performance is driven by frequent claims or expensive claims.
The workflow then moves from portfolio-level analysis to segment-level analysis and advanced visual analytics. This structure supports a clear analytical logic: first identifying the overall profitability trend, then locating high-risk segments, and finally translating the findings into pricing, underwriting, and tail-risk monitoring implications.

title: Take-Home_Ex01
text:
This section uses portfolio-level visual analytics to examine the overall profitability trend of the insurance portfolio. The analysis begins with yearly aggregation because the raw dataset is policy-level, while profitability deterioration is easier to observe at the portfolio-year level.
The group_by() and summarise() functions in the dplyr package are used to aggregate total premium, total incurred claims, total claims, and exposure by year. The ggplot() function in the ggplot2 package is then used to create bar charts comparing yearly loss ratios and yearly premium-claim movements. The scales package is used to format loss ratios as percentages and monetary values as currency.



The dataset is suitable for motor insurance portfolio analysis because it contains premium income, incurred claims, claim counts, exposure, policy characteristics, driver information, and vehicle information.
Several insurance-specific analytical variables are created, including profit, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, and claim_severity. These variables transform the raw data into a more meaningful analytical sandbox for profitability and risk analysis.
Driver age, vehicle age, and vehicle value are grouped into categorical segments to support clearer visual comparison across risk groups.





portfolio_summary <- motor_clean %>%
  summarise(
    number_of_records = n(),
    unique_insured = n_distinct(insured_id),
    total_premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    overall_profit = total_premium - total_incurred,
    overall_loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium,
    overall_claim_frequency = total_claims / total_exposure,
    overall_claim_severity = total_incurred / total_claims
  )

portfolio_summary

# A tibble: 1 × 10
  number_of_records unique_insured total_premium total_incurred total_claims
              <int>          <int>         <dbl>          <dbl>        <dbl>
1            352338         184724    104379210.      73410702.        76542
# ℹ 5 more variables: total_exposure <dbl>, overall_profit <dbl>,
#   overall_loss_ratio <dbl>, overall_claim_frequency <dbl>,
#   overall_claim_severity <dbl>


The portfolio-level summary provides the baseline for the whole analysis. At the aggregate level, the portfolio appears profitable because total premium income is higher than total incurred claims. However, this aggregate result should not be interpreted as evidence that every segment is performing well.
In insurance portfolio analysis, the overall loss ratio can hide large differences across product types, customer groups, vehicle characteristics, and policy behaviours. A portfolio can be profitable overall while still containing loss-making subgroups. Therefore, the following sections move from portfolio-level analysis to segment-level analysis to identify where profitability problems and claim volatility are concentrated.




year_summary <- motor_clean %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    profit = premium - incurred,
    loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    claim_severity = incurred / claims,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

year_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 9
   year   premium  incurred claims exposure    profit loss_ratio claim_frequency
  <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>           <dbl>
1  2022 18596245. 12219605.  12613   41741.  6376639.      0.657           0.302
2  2023 35125315. 23371029.  24992   82014. 11754285.      0.665           0.305
3  2024 50657651. 37820067.  38937  125317. 12837584.      0.747           0.311
# ℹ 1 more variable: claim_severity <dbl>



The plotThe Code














ggplot(year_summary, aes(x = factor(year), y = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)),
    vjust = -0.3,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent,
    limits = c(0, 1.1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Portfolio Loss Ratio by Year",
    subtitle = "The dashed line represents the 100% break-even loss ratio",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Loss Ratio"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()




The yearly loss ratio shows a clear upward trend from 2022 to 2024. The loss ratio increased from 65.7% in 2022 to 66.5% in 2023, and then rose more noticeably to 74.7% in 2024. Since loss ratio measures incurred claims as a proportion of premium income, this increase suggests that claim costs are growing faster than premium income.
Although the portfolio remains profitable overall because the loss ratio is still below 100%, the upward trend indicates weaker profitability over time. This is an important warning signal for the insurer because it may reflect higher claim frequency, higher claim severity, claim inflation, or insufficient premium adjustment.
Therefore, the later sections examine claim frequency, claim severity, and segment-level loss ratios to identify which factors may be driving the deterioration in portfolio profitability.




The plotThe Code














year_long <- year_summary %>%
  select(year, premium, incurred) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(premium, incurred),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "amount"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      "premium" = "Premium Income",
      "incurred" = "Incurred Claims"
    )
  )

ggplot(year_long, aes(x = factor(year), y = amount, fill = metric)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  labs(
    title = "Premium Income and Incurred Claims by Year",
    subtitle = "Both premium and claims increased, but claim costs grew faster in 2024",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Amount",
    fill = "Metric"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()




This chart compares premium income and incurred claims across the three policy years. Both premium income and incurred claims increased from 2022 to 2024, indicating that the portfolio became larger over time. However, incurred claims increased more rapidly relative to premium income, especially in 2024.
In 2022 and 2023, the gap between premium income and incurred claims remained relatively wide. In 2024, although premium income reached its highest level, incurred claims also increased substantially. This explains why the loss ratio rose to 74.7% in 2024.
From a portfolio management perspective, this pattern suggests that business growth alone does not guarantee stronger profitability. If claim costs grow faster than premium income, the insurer’s underwriting margin becomes thinner. Therefore, it is important to investigate whether the increase in incurred claims is driven by higher claim frequency, higher claim severity, or specific high-risk segments.
Business growth does not necessarily improve profitability if claim costs grow faster than premium income.

year_growth <- year_summary %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(
    premium_growth = premium / lag(premium) - 1,
    incurred_growth = incurred / lag(incurred) - 1
  ) %>%
  select(year, premium_growth, incurred_growth)

year_growth

   year premium_growth incurred_growth
