section: 5.1 Selecting the top six source countries
text:
5.1 Selecting the top six source countries
The teacher example compares the top four countries using raw attack counts. My analysis expands the comparison to six countries and calculates within-country percentages. This prevents countries with larger attack volumes from dominating the visual interpretation.

top6 <- attacks_by_country %>%
  slice_head(n = 6) %>%
  pull(source_country)

top6_profile <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top6) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  group_by(source_country) %>%
  mutate(
    country_total = sum(n),
    share = n / country_total
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    source_country = factor(
      source_country,
      levels = top6
    )
  ) %>%
  drop_na()

title: Hands-on Exercise: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
5.2 Plotting normalised calendar heatmaps

ggplot(
  top6_profile,
  aes(x = hour, y = wkday, fill = share)
) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1),
    name = "Share of each\ncountry's attacks"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    title = "Normalised Attack Timing Profiles for the Top Six Source Countries",
    subtitle = "Each heatmap shows the within-country percentage distribution of attacks"
  ) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Arial") +
  theme(
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 6),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )

title: Hands-on Exercise: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
5.3 Identifying peak attack periods

peak_attack_periods <- top6_profile %>%
  group_by(source_country) %>%
  slice_max(
    order_by = n,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  transmute(
    source_country,
    peak_weekday = wkday,
    peak_hour = as.character(hour),
    attacks = n,
    within_country_share = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)
  )

DT::datatable(
  peak_attack_periods,
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 6,
    dom = "tip"
  )
)

title: Hands-on Exercise: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
5.4 Comparing the busiest hours

peak_attack_periods %>%
  mutate(
    peak_hour = as.numeric(peak_hour),
    source_country = fct_reorder(source_country, peak_hour)
  ) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = peak_hour,
      y = source_country
    )
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = 0,
      xend = peak_hour,
      yend = source_country
    ),
    linewidth = 0.8,
    colour = "grey70"
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:23) +
  labs(
    x = "Peak Hour of Day",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Peak Attack Hour for Each Leading Source Country"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Arial")

title: Hands-on Exercise: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
5.5 Interpretation
The normalised heatmaps support fairer comparisons across countries because the colour scale represents each country’s internal attack distribution rather than its absolute number of attacks. The peak-period table and lollipop chart make the most active time window easier to identify.

selected_market <- air %>%

section: 7.1 Selecting the earliest and latest years
text:
7.1 Selecting the earliest and latest years
Instead of using a fixed pair of years, I compare the earliest and latest years available in the rice dataset. This makes the analysis reusable if the dataset is updated.

first_year <- min(rice$Year, na.rm = TRUE)
last_year <- max(rice$Year, na.rm = TRUE)

c(first_year, last_year)

[1] 1961 2010

title: Hands-on Exercise: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
7.2 Computing yield changes

rice_change <- rice %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(first_year, last_year)) %>%
  group_by(Country) %>%
  summarise(
    start_yield = Yield[Year == first_year][1],
    end_yield = Yield[Year == last_year][1],
    yield_change = end_yield - start_yield,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  drop_na()

top_change_countries <- rice_change %>%
  slice_max(
    order_by = abs(yield_change),
    n = 10,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

title: Hands-on Exercise: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
7.3 Plotting the yield-change bar chart

top_change_countries %>%
  mutate(
    Country = fct_reorder(Country, yield_change)
  ) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = yield_change,
      y = Country,
      fill = yield_change > 0
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(
    x = paste("Yield Change:", first_year, "to", last_year),
    y = NULL,
    title = "Countries with the Largest Long-term Rice Yield Changes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Arial")

title: Hands-on Exercise: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
7.4 Plotting a focused slopegraph

rice_long_term <- rice %>%
  filter(
    Country %in% top_change_countries$Country,
    Year %in% c(first_year, last_year)
  ) %>%
  mutate(Year = factor(Year))

ggplot(
  rice_long_term,
  aes(
    x = Year,
    y = Yield,
    group = Country
  )
) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = Country),
    direction = "y",
    size = 3,
    max.overlaps = Inf,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Rice Yield",
    title = "Long-term Rice Yield Change for Selected Countries",
    subtitle = paste(first_year, "to", last_year)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Arial")

DT::datatable(
  top_change_countries %>%
    arrange(desc(abs(yield_change))),

  options = list(
    pageLength = 10,
    dom = "tip"
  )

The bar chart quickly identifies the countries with the largest long-term increases or decreases in yield. The slopegraph then shows the direction and magnitude of change in a compact visual form. Using the earliest and latest available years provides a broader view than the fixed two-year teacher example.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9b: Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
This hands-on exercise follows the learning flow of Chapter 22 from R for Visual Analytics. The teacher example focuses on visualising Singapore Pools outlets as geospatial point data. The main visualisation method is the proportional symbol map, where the size of each point symbol represents the magnitude of a numeric variable.
In this file, I first reproduce the teacher example. Then, in the Self Trying section, I extend the analysis by looking at high-winning outlets, zero-winning outlets, outlet type differences, and spatial concentration patterns.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9b: Visualising Geospatial Point Data
section: 5 Self Trying: Exploring Winning Intensity of Singapore Pools Outlets
text:
5 Self Trying: Exploring Winning Intensity of Singapore Pools Outlets
In this self-trying section, I use the same geospatial point data, but the analysis focus is different from the teacher example. Instead of only mapping all outlets, I try to identify where high-winning outlets are located and whether branches and outlets show different spatial patterns.

5.1 Preparing analysis variables
I first create several variables that make the analysis easier to read. I classify outlets into winning intensity groups and also identify whether an outlet has no Group 1 or Group 2 winnings.


Code
sgpools_self <- sgpools_sf %>%
  mutate(
    winnings = `Gp1Gp2 Winnings`,
    win_status = if_else(winnings == 0, "No winnings", "At least one winning"),
    win_class = case_when(
      winnings == 0 ~ "0",
      winnings <= 10 ~ "1-10",
      winnings <= 25 ~ "11-25",
      winnings <= 50 ~ "26-50",
      TRUE ~ "Above 50"
    ),
    win_class = factor(
      win_class,
      levels = c("0", "1-10", "11-25", "26-50", "Above 50")
    )
  )

sgpools_self



  





5.2 Summary of outlet type and winnings
Before drawing the map, I summarise the number of outlets and winnings by outlet type.


Code
outlet_summary <- sgpools_self %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(`OUTLET TYPE`) %>%
  summarise(
    outlets = n(),
    total_winnings = sum(winnings, na.rm = TRUE),
    average_winnings = mean(winnings, na.rm = TRUE),
    zero_winning_outlets = sum(winnings == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

outlet_summary



  





Code
DT::datatable(
  outlet_summary,
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10,
    autoWidth = TRUE
  )
)








5.3 Bar chart of winnings by outlet type
This chart complements the map by comparing the total number of Group 1 and Group 2 winnings by outlet type.


Code
outlet_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `OUTLET TYPE`, y = total_winnings, fill = `OUTLET TYPE`)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = total_winnings), vjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Group 1 and Group 2 Winnings by Outlet Type",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Total winnings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")











5.4 Self Trying Map 1: Winning intensity map
This map uses both colour and size. Colour shows the winning intensity class, while symbol size represents the actual number of winnings.


Code
tmap_mode("view")

win_palette <- c(
  "0" = "grey75",
  "1-10" = "#a6cee3",
  "11-25" = "#1f78b4",
  "26-50" = "#fb9a99",
  "Above 50" = "#e31a1c"
)

tm_shape(sgpools_self) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "win_class",
    size = "winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 0.6,
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = win_palette),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Winning class"),
    size.legend = tm_legend(title = "Winnings")
  )










5.5 Self Trying Map 2: High-winning outlets only
The next map focuses only on outlets with more than 50 winnings. This makes it easier to see where the strongest winning locations are located.


Code
high_winning <- sgpools_self %>%
  filter(winnings > 50)

high_winning



  





Code
tm_shape(high_winning) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
    size = "winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 0.8,
    size.legend = tm_legend(title = "Winnings"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Outlet type")
  )










5.6 Self Trying Map 3: Zero-winning versus winning outlets
This map compares outlets with no winnings and outlets with at least one winning. It helps to show whether zero-winning outlets are spatially concentrated or spread across Singapore.


Code
tm_shape(sgpools_self) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "win_status",
    size = 0.7,
    col = "black",
    lwd = 0.4,
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Winning status")
  )









5.7 Faceted map by winning class
This small multiple map separates outlets by winning intensity. Compared with a single crowded map, the faceted version makes it easier to compare low-, medium-, and high-winning outlets.


Code
tm_shape(sgpools_self) +
  tm_bubbles(
    fill = "win_class",
    size = "winnings",
    col = "black",
    lwd = 0.5,
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = win_palette)
  ) +
  tm_facets(
    by = "win_class",
    nrow = 1,
    sync = TRUE
  )





































5.8 Top 15 winning outlets
The table below lists the top 15 outlets by Group 1 and Group 2 winnings.


Code
top15_winning <- sgpools_self %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(desc(winnings)) %>%
  select(
    NAME,
    ADDRESS,
    POSTCODE,
    `OUTLET TYPE`,
    winnings,
    win_class
  ) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

DT::datatable(
  top15_winning,
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 15,
    autoWidth = TRUE
  )
)








5.9 Interpretation
From the self-trying maps, I can compare three aspects of the point data. First, the proportional symbol map shows that a small number of outlets have much higher winning counts than most outlets. Second, mapping only high-winning outlets reduces visual clutter and makes spatial concentration easier to observe. Third, comparing zero-winning and winning outlets shows whether low-performing outlets are randomly distributed or appear in certain areas. The faceted map further improves readability by separating outlets into different winning classes.


Code
tmap_mode("plot")

title: Hands-on Exercise 10: Information Dashboard Design with R
text:
2.2 Importing prepared RDS data
The code below reads the prepared Coffee Chain data. If the RDS file is not available, a small synthetic Coffee Chain-like data set is created so that the file can still render.


Code
if (file.exists("data/rds/CoffeeChain.rds")) {
  coffeechain <- read_rds("data/rds/CoffeeChain.rds")
} else {
  set.seed(1234)
  dir.create("data/rds", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  product_names <- c(
    "Amaretto", "Caffe Latte", "Caffe Mocha", "Chamomile",
    "Colombian", "Darjeeling", "Decaf Espresso", "Decaf Irish Cream",
    "Earl Grey", "Green Tea", "Lemon", "Mint", "Regular Espresso"
  )
  coffeechain <- expand_grid(
    Date = seq.Date(as.Date("2012-01-01"), as.Date("2013-12-01"), by = "month"),
    Product = product_names
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      `Product Type` = case_when(
        str_detect(Product, "Caffe|Espresso") ~ "Coffee",
        str_detect(Product, "Tea|Chamomile|Darjeeling|Earl|Mint|Lemon") ~ "Tea",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      ),
      base_sales = case_when(
        Product %in% c("Colombian", "Lemon", "Caffe Mocha") ~ 5000,
        Product %in% c("Chamomile", "Darjeeling", "Decaf Espresso") ~ 3200,
        TRUE ~ 1500
      ),
      seasonal = 1 + 0.12 * sin(2 * pi * month(Date) / 12),
      Sales = round(base_sales * seasonal + rnorm(n(), 0, 180)),
      `Budget Sales` = round(base_sales * runif(n(), 0.95, 1.15))
    ) %>%
    select(Date, Product, `Product Type`, Sales, `Budget Sales`)
  write_rds(coffeechain, "data/rds/CoffeeChain.rds")
}

8.1 Creating product performance indicators


Code
self_product <- coffeechain %>%
  mutate(
    Year = year(Date),
    Month = month(Date)
  ) %>%
  filter(Year == 2013) %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(
    Actual = sum(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    Target = sum(`Budget Sales`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Average_Monthly_Sales = mean(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    Sales_SD = sd(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    Best_Month = Month[which.max(Sales)],
    Worst_Month = Month[which.min(Sales)],
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Achievement = Actual / Target,
    Gap = Actual - Target,
    Volatility = Sales_SD / Average_Monthly_Sales,
    Status = case_when(
      Achievement >= 1.05 ~ "Above target",
      Achievement >= 0.95 ~ "Near target",
      TRUE ~ "Below target"
    ),
    Status = factor(Status, levels = c("Above target", "Near target", "Below target"))
  )

          list(fontWeight = "bold", color = "#b2182b")
        } else if (value == "Medium priority") {
          list(fontWeight = "bold", color = "#ef8a62")
        } else {
          list(color = "#4d4d4d")
        }
      }
    )
  )

text:
8.7 Interpretation
The self-trying dashboard combines three types of performance evidence. The bullet chart compares actual sales with budgeted sales, the sparkline shows monthly movement, and the priority table highlights products that are below target or volatile. This design is more useful than a single chart because it supports both high-level monitoring and product-level diagnosis.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Insight 1
Insight 1 - Portfolio Profitability Deteriorated in 2024


Loss ratio increased from 65.7% in 2022 to 74.7% in 2024.
The portfolio remains profitable, but the underwriting margin became thinner.
The 2024 deterioration motivates deeper frequency-severity and segment-level analysis.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Insight 2
Insight 2 - Premium Growth Did Not Fully Offset Claim Growth


Both premium income and incurred claims increased from 2022 to 2024.
Incurred claims grew faster relative to premium income in 2024.
Business growth does not necessarily improve profitability if claim costs grow faster.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Insight 3
Insight 3 - Claim Risk is Concentrated in Large-Loss Policies


Claim costs are highly concentrated among high-loss policies.
Portfolio volatility is strongly influenced by tail-risk observations.
Large-loss policies should be monitored separately from average claim behavior.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Insight 4a
Insight 4 - COMP_N is the Highest-Risk Policy Type

title: Executive Summary
text:
Insight 4b


COMP_N has the highest loss ratio at 93.5%.
It also has the highest claim frequency at 1.04.
This suggests that COMP_N is a frequency-driven high-risk segment.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Insight 5
Insight 5 - Policy Status C is Loss-Making


Policy status C has a loss ratio of 128.0%.
This segment is loss-making because claim costs exceed premium income.
Policy closure or cancellation may be associated with adverse claim experience.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Insight 6
Insight 6 - Diesel Vehicles are Frequency-Driven Risk


Diesel vehicles have higher claim frequency than gasoline vehicles.
Claim severity is almost identical between the two groups.
The fuel-type difference is mainly frequency-driven rather than severity-driven.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Insight 7
Insight 7 - High Risk is Concentrated in COMP_N + Semi-Annual Payment


COMP_N + S has a loss ratio of 108.8%.
This specific product-payment combination is loss-making.
Segment-level visual analytics reveals risks hidden in one-variable summaries.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Insight 8
Insight 8 - Premium Adequacy Quadrant Confirms COMP_N Risk


COMP_N is located in the high-frequency and high-loss-ratio area.
COMP_E is also above the portfolio average on both dimensions.
CC and TP appear to be stronger-performing segments.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Recommendations
Recommendations Pricing and Underwriting Priorities

Review pricing and underwriting rules for COMP_N.
Prioritise investigation of COMP_N + S, since it is loss-making.
Monitor policy status C, which has a loss ratio above 100%.
Treat diesel vehicles as a frequency-driven risk segment.
Add tail-risk monitoring for large-loss policies.
Monitor yearly loss ratio movement to detect pricing inadequacy earlier.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Final Takeaway
Final Takeaway Visual analytics identifies where profitability problems are concentrated

The portfolio remains profitable overall.
Profitability deteriorated in 2024.
Claim risk is concentrated in specific segments.
COMP_N, policy status C, and COMP_N + S are the most important risk signals.
Visual analytics supports more targeted pricing, underwriting, and portfolio monitoring.

title: MC2 Data description
text:
This folder contains the data for the anomalous postings originating from Tenant Thread.
This data is based on the actions taken by the employees and personal agents inside of Tenant Thread.


The anomalous posting is sent to SaidIt by John Windward on May 17, 2046 at 4:21am.



MC2_Data.json – A timeline of events gathered by the internal systems. org_chart.json – The organization chart of Tenant Thread including people and departments. Compatible with networkX node_link_graph.



Derived from data:
{
   "description": "string",
   "events": [
      {
         "short_name": "string",
         "parties": "array",
         "when": "float",
         "details": "object",
         "id": "int"
      }
   ]
}



The data is structured as a timeline. The events are ordered and indicate the operations performed by people, autonomous agents and office systems.
Field meanings: - short_name: The action taken - parties: Which people/agents/systems were involved. - when: Unix timestamp. The challenge occurs in May 2046, and timestamps should be in that month. - details: Additional information about the action taken. The contents vary by the contents of short_name. - id: A unique id for each record.
